title: Zoho Skips Annual Pay Hikes as AI Costs Surge, Vembu Warns on Software Jobs
excerpt: Sridhar Vembu blamed a fourfold jump in server prices and rising AI usage costs, said headcount has been flat for 18 months, and apologised to employees — while vowing to avoid mass layoffs.
body:
• Zoho will not give its usual annual salary increase this year, founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu announced in a post on X, apologising to employees.
  • Vembu blamed a fourfold increase in server prices for Zoho's data centres and rapidly rising AI usage costs; the company has also cut its marketing budget.
  • Zoho's headcount has not grown for 18 months, and Vembu said the company will work hard to avoid mass layoffs — but called the outlook for software jobs in general "grim."
  • For Indian tech workers, including the diaspora engineers who anchor the industry, the signal is that AI infrastructure spending is now crowding out pay rises and hiring even at profitable, bootstrapped firms.

Zoho Corporation will skip its usual annual salary hike this year, founder Sridhar Vembu announced in a post on X, citing a dramatic rise in artificial intelligence costs and an uncertain outlook for the software business. "The business outlook for software is uncertain and AI has raised costs dramatically," Vembu wrote, pointing to a "massive 4-fold increase in server prices which we need for data centers" and rapidly increasing AI usage expenses, according to Hindustan Times.

"We have cut down on our marketing budget. We have also told our employees that we cannot have our usual pay increase this year. I have apologized for not being able to avoid this," he wrote.

A hiring freeze already in place

The pay decision is not Zoho's first retrenchment. Vembu said the company has not grown its employee count for 18 months. Zoho, one of India's largest privately held software companies, is bootstrapped and has long marketed its frugality and rural hiring model as an alternative to venture-funded rivals — which makes its cost squeeze a pointed signal for the wider industry.

"We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs but the outlook for software jobs in general is grim."

— Sridhar Vembu, Founder, Zoho

The wider AI jobs argument

Vembu's announcement landed alongside a broader set of posts in which he argued that AI-driven job losses require new kinds of human work rather than a universal basic income, which he has called dystopian, according to India Today and Rediff. His recurring theme: as AI automates intellectual work, value shifts to work machines cannot do — care, craft, farming and local services. Whether or not one accepts that framing, his own company's payroll is now Exhibit A for the cost side of the transition: money that once funded raises and hiring is going to servers and AI usage instead.

What it means for tech workers

For software employees in India and the diaspora, the Zoho move matters less for its size than for its source. This is not a loss-making startup cutting to survive; it is a profitable product company choosing infrastructure over increments. Workers weighing offers in 2026-27 should expect the same trade-off across the sector: flat headcounts, selective hiring at the senior end, and compensation growth concentrated in AI-adjacent roles — a pattern already visible in industry hiring data.

What's next

Vembu gave no timeline for restoring hikes and disclosed neither the size of Zoho's AI cost increase nor how many employees are affected. The next signals will come from India's listed IT majors as they report this earnings season — and from whether Zoho's hiring freeze, now at 18 months, extends into a second full year.
